name: Gnosticism
plain_explanation: A set of religious movements that held the material world was created by an inferior, flawed deity (not the true supreme God), and that Christ's mission was to free people from this inferior creator's false teaching -- often identifying that inferior creator with the Old Testament's Yahweh.
precise_definition: A family of syncretic sects holding, in one influential version, that the sensible world was created by an inferior deity (Ialdabaoth, identified with Yahweh), that the serpent of Genesis was benevolent, and that the supreme deity's Son temporarily inhabited the body of Jesus to liberate the world from Mosaic teaching; typically combined with Platonic philosophy.
why_it_mattered: It offered a 'half-way house' between philosophic paganism and Christianity for cultivated Greek-speaking converts uncomfortable with Jewish particularism, since it honored Christ while disparaging the Jews; it also directly influenced a doctrine later adopted by Islam.
historical_origin: Flourished especially before Christianity became the state religion; continued a subterranean influence after being suppressed.
examples: The Docetic sect's view that a mere phantom, not Jesus himself, hung on the cross, later adopted by Islam
The New Testament's own warning in 1 Timothy against 'oppositions of science falsely so called'
objections: Orthodox Christianity rejected it explicitly, e.g., in the Pastoral Epistles' warning against 'Gnosis falsely so called'
Plotinus, from the pagan Platonist side, also found it necessary to refute Gnostic doctrines
competing_positions: Manichaeism (a related but distinct dualist system)
influence_on_later_thinkers: The Docetic view of Christ's crucifixion passed, via a Gnostic sect, into orthodox Islamic doctrine about Jesus.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: A religious movement with an implicit anti-Jewish theological edge that Russell connects to broader early Christian hostility to Jews.
